fit.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = bifactor.model, data = CFA, ordered = TRUE, parameterization = "theta", estimator = "WLSMV", ID.fac = "UV", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016", group = "Gender", return.fit = TRUE)

I want to test a mediation model using path analysis and compare the mediation on the three groups on a model with 2IVs, 2 Mediators and 2 DVs. First, I have fitted a direct model (2 IVs predicting 2 DVs + covariances between the two IVs and the two DVs) and use the command group="Condition". The results obtained in R look like this:

Regressions:

I am assuming that the multigroup command is fitting the model to each group independently, right? Should I be using a different command to fit the model independently to each group or subset of the data?

I am able to compare if the models are significantly different from each other as I would do with a two group model? What does the p value highlighted is indicating? messages.body_plain:
Olaya--
     Your syntax would be better than your results as a guide to what analysis was conducted, though there are clues.
     You *did* get chi-squares for all three groups, but chi-square was 0 for 2 of the groups. If this is real data, then random sampling error would keep chi-square from being exactly 0 unless the model is saturated (degrees of freedom or DF = 0). Therefore, the model you actually estimated was saturated in 2 groups but had 2 effective constraints in one group.
     In addition, if the model were the same in all 3 groups but estimated separately in each group, then degrees of freedom would have to be a multiple of 3--DF in a single group times 3 groups. With 2 DF total, this cannot be so.
     Therefore, your syntax produced a model with 2 constraints in 1 group and saturation in the others. The model that you describe--2 predictors with direct effects on 2 outcome variables, with residual covariance between predictors and between outcomes--sounds saturated to me, so DF should be 0. So it seems most likely that there is an error in your syntax involving the first group. With that error resolved, however, chi-square will be 0 for all 3 groups, because the model will be saturated in all 3 groups.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
Olaya--
     The model is now fully saturated. With 0 degrees of freedom, the model must fit the data perfectly, as indicated by chi-square = 0. The baseline chi-square only tells you that the "independence model" (all observed variables mutually uncorrelated) does not fit well. So you cannot tell from these fit index results whether there are any "statistically significant" differences across models. Depending on what you mean by "differences," you might impose across-group constraints and thus obtain positive degrees of freedom and a basis for conducting statistical tests.
--Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
> 1) whether the specification below is correct?

Mostly, but you have omitted the between-component of time from your level-2 model, which might incorrectly assumes it is uncorrelated with everything else at level 2.

> 2) specifically with respect to the 2-2-1 mediation (group_time -> K1 -> IE2), wether I should specify something like indirect := ba*wb?

No. Process at different levels are independent, they do not cross levels.

Preacher, K. J., Zyphur, M. J., & Zhang, Z. (2010). A general multilevel SEM framework for assessing multilevel mediation. Psychological Methods, 15, 209-233.

Preacher, K. J., Zhang, Z., & Zyphur, M. J. (2011). Alternative methods for assessing mediation in multilevel data: The advantages of multilevel SEM. Structural Equation Modeling, 18, 161- 182.

> 3) related to that: do I interprete the b-path at level 2 for the "group_time -> K1 -> IE2"-mediation?

Like any other indirect effect, but involving group means.  Read the articles above to learn about these models.

messages.subject_clean: lavaan Regression predictors p values different than the SPSS output
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am running a regression based on covariances matrix with two predictors, PS and PC (script to follow).
All is working as intended but I get slightly different p-values for PS (p = .082) and PC (p = .013) than the SPSS values.
Any ideas on why this happens?

Many thanks in advance.

script:

# Y : Dv
# PS, PC predictors (k:2 predictors, plus 1 intercept)

# N contains 100 onservations

N <- 100
k <-2

#define correlation matrix
cor_matrix =
matrix(
  c(
   1, 0.1, -0.2,
   0.1, 1,  0.3,
  -0.2, 0.3, 1
), nrow = 3, ncol = 3,
dimnames = list(
  c("Y", "PS", "PC"),
  c("Y", "PS", "PC")
))

# convert correlation matrix to covvariance matrix for lavaan
library(lavaan)
sd_vector = c(1,1,1)
mean_vector = c(0,0,0)
cov_matrix = lavaan::cor2cov(cor_matrix, sd_vector)

# fit the model
fit <- sem( "Y ~ PS + PC",
           sample.cov = cov_matrix,
           sample.nobs = N,
           meanstructure = TRUE,
           sample.mean = mean_vector)

# get Rsquare
inspect(fit, "r2")
R2 <-inspect(fit, "r2")

# get F-statistic and p-value
fvalue <-((R2)*(N-k-1))/((1-R2)*(k))
cat("F = ", fvalue)
pvalue <- pf(fvalue, k, N-k-1, lower.tail = FALSE)
cat("p = ", pvalue)

# look at the regression
summary(fit, standardize=TRUE, rsquare = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
> is the R2 generated when rsq=TRUE referring to the McKelvey & Zavoina's pseudo R2

Yes.

> or to an OLS regression R2?

The only difference is that in OLS the Y is observed so the error variance can be estimated instead of fixed.  McKelvey & Zavoina's R^2 is interpreted as the proportion of variance in the *latent* Y that is explained by predictors, rather than the OLS R^2 being the proportion of the observed Y's variance explained by predictors.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics

messages.subject: Re: lavaan Regression predictors p values different than the SPSS output
messages.subject_clean: lavaan Regression predictors p values different than the SPSS output
messages.body_plain:
> I get slightly different p-values for PS (p = .082) and PC (p = .013) than the SPSS values.
> Any ideas on why this happens?

The point estimates are the same because OLS estimates are ML estimates when OLS assumptions are met.  But MLE is more efficient, so its SEs are smaller, affecting the t or Wald z ratio and p values.  Also, even if the SEs were identical, the p value would differ because MLE is asymptotic, whereas OLS is not; in the latter, the df parameter for an approximately normal t distribution can be derived, instead of relying on an asymptotic Wald z statistic being perfectly normal even in finite samples.

FYI, you can simulate data that conform perfectly to your summary stats if you just want to use lm()

simData <- MASS::mvrnorm(N, mu = mean_vector, Sigma = cov_matrix,
                         empirical = TRUE)
summary(lm(Y ~ PS + PC, data = data.frame(simData))) # same slopes and R^2

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

No idea what is going on. Most likely, this is not related to lavaan.
Just 3 suggestions:

1) use lavaan::cfa() instead of cfa() to make sure you are calling
lavaan's cfa()

2) type at the R console

sink()

to make sure no connections are still open.

3) open vanilla R (not RStudio) and try it there

Yves.

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrance and all,

First, thank you for the thorough and informative response, it's been very helpful. I tried to write the syntax for the model and I would appreciate feedback on it.
As I've mentioned in the previous email, the DV were measured at level-1, while independent variables were measured at either level-1 or level-2.
What I am unsure about is whether I need to specify the level-1 DVs in the level-2 equation?
Here is my syntax:
m1 <- '
Level: 1
TV ~ ndt*NDVI_ind + vht*Veg_height + vct*Veg_cover + nt*Neighbors + rt*Rosette + mt*Mass + wt*Width
Width ~ ndw*NDVI_ind + vhw*Veg_height + vcw*Veg_cover + nw*Neighbors + rw*Rosette + mw*Mass
Mass ~ ndm*NDVI_ind + vhm*Veg_height + vcm*Veg_cover + nm*Neighbors + rm*Rosette
SRH ~ nds*NDVI_ind + vhs*Veg_height + vcs*Veg_cover + ns*Neighbors + rs*Rosette
Rosette ~ ndr*NDVI_ind + vhr*Veg_height + vcr*Veg_cover + nr*Neighbors
Neighbors ~ ndn*NDVI_ind + vhn*Veg_height + vcn*Veg_cover
Veg_height ~ ndvh*NDVI_ind + vcvh*Veg_cover
Veg_cover ~ ndvc*NDVI_ind

Level: 2
TV ~ at*Area + ct*Con
Width ~ aw*Area + cw*Con
Mass ~ am*Area + cm* Con
SRH ~ as*Area + cs*Con
Rosette ~ ar*Area + cr*Con
Neighbors ~ an*Area + cn*Con
Veg_height ~ avh*Area + cvh*Con
Veg_cover ~ avc*Area + cvc*Con
NDVI_ind ~ and*Area + cnd*Con
Area ~~ Con
'

So, for example, to model the effect on TV, do I need to include in the level-2 equation NDVI, Veg_height, and all the other DVs that appear in the level-1 TV equation?
And if so, should I parameterize them with the same path coefficients as they have in the level-1 equation, or with new ones?

Thanks for the help!
Efrat

On Mon, Sep 23, 2019 at 11:24 PM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > 1. Would it be more appropriate to account for the nestedness of the data by using a multilevel model in lavaan and using the patches as clusters, or to use lavaan.survey?
>
> lavaan.survey() only corrects SEs and tests for clustering in a level-1 model (also available in lavaan() now, if you specify a cluster= variable for a single-level model).  You have Level-2 hypotheses (a patch-level IV predicts the patch-level component of an individual-level IV), so MLSEM seems more appropriate.
>
> > 2. What are the appropriate fit indices to look at for multilevel models?
>
> All the same fit indices are available, but it is recommended to evaluate fit at each level separately.  SRMRs are available at each level of analysis.
>
> > 3. Are there any recommended packages for plotting lavaan models? Semplot works poorly when there are many variables and connections.
>
> And I think it only plots MLSEMs from Mplus output; not sure about OpenMx or lavaan yet.
>
> > 4. Is there an efficient way to estimate direct, indirect and total effects in lavaan? I know one can add equations in the syntax to do that, but for complex models this can be quite tedious.
>
> No, but you can check to see if you missed any by multiplying the beta matrix (at either level) against itself 2, then 3, then ... p-1 times (the maximum number of sequential causal links).
>
> B <- lavInspect(fit, "est")[[1]]$beta # level-1 beta
> B %*% B        # 2-path indirect effects
> B %*% B %*% B  # 3-path indirect effects
>
>
> By the time you get a product full of zeros, you won't have any more indirect effects of higher order.  Each nonzero cell is the point estimate for an indirect effect whose path you can trace from the predictor (column variable) to the outcome (row variable).  To obtain the delta-method SEs, you can check that each nonzero cell in each product is represented in your model syntax.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> What I am unsure about is whether I need to specify the level-1 DVs in the level-2 equation?

Every level-1 variable has a level-2 component (i.e., the cluster means) whose variance can only be modeled at level 2.  If you have no hypotheses about it, you could just allow it to covary with everything else at level 2, but it should be accounted for in your syntax

> should I parameterize them with the same path coefficients as they have in the level-1 equation, or with new ones?

Are you asking whether they need to be equal across levels?  No, process across levels can look very different.  Level-1 and -2 models do not have to have the same form, nor equal estimates of any parameters that are in both models.  But the data must be modeled (i.e., level-1 variables have level-2 components, period).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Differents results under lavaan (R) and Lisrel
messages.subject_clean: Differents results under lavaan (R) and Lisrel
messages.body_plain:
> In both programs I used a diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS)

So you have ordered outcomes?  LISREL handles those by fixing the first threshold to zero and (if there are > 2 categories) the second threshold to one, in order to identify the means and variances of the (assumed normally distributed) latent responses underlying each binary/ordinal endogenous variable.  For binary outcomes, the fixed threshold only identifies the mean, so the variance is fixed to 1.  Furthermore, if you have multiple groups, any estimated thresholds are equated across groups, period (assumed, not tested).

This is quite different from Mplus and lavaan's default behavior, which estimates all thresholds, fixing any latent response's mean/intercept to zero and its total (parameterization = "delta") or residual (parameterization = "theta") variance to 1.  Given those threshold estimates, polychoric/polyserial correlations are estimated.

https://doi.org/10.1207/S15327906MBR3903_4

A consequence of these differences is that LISREL and Mplus/lavaan are trying to reproduce different data. The latter are trying to reproduce the estimated (thresholds and) correlation matrix, whereas LISREL is trying to reproduce an estimated covariance matrix (given some fixed thresholds).  I expect these approaches should be statistically equivalent (see lavaan example below comparing approaches, although lavaan's fit criterion still is not LISREL's), which would be consistent with the equal df = 48.  Perhaps their results differ because the criterion for choosing estimates differs... I would input LISREL's model-implied covariance matrix into R, transform it to a correlation matrix using cov2cor(), then compare that to lavaan's model-implied correlation matrix: lavInspect(fit, "cor.ov")

syntax.mplus <- ' Factor =~ u1 + u2 + u3 + u4 '
fit.mplus <- cfa(syntax.mplus, data = datCat,
                 ordered = paste0("u", 1:4), parameterization = "theta")
syntax.lisrel <- c(syntax.mplus, '## THRESHOLDS:
    u1 | 0*t1 + 1*t2 + NA*t3 + NA*t4
    u2 | 0*t1 + 1*t2 + NA*t3 + NA*t4
    u3 | 0*t1 + 1*t2 + NA*t3 + NA*t4
    u4 | 0*t1 + 1*t2 + NA*t3 + NA*t4

    ## INTERCEPTS:
    u1 ~ NA*1
    u2 ~ NA*1
    u3 ~ NA*1
    u4 ~ NA*1

    ## UNIQUE-FACTOR VARIANCES:
    u1 ~~ NA*u1
    u2 ~~ NA*u2
    u3 ~~ NA*u3
    u4 ~~ NA*u4
')
fit.lisrel <- cfa(syntax.lisrel, data = datCat,
                 ordered = paste0("u", 1:4), parameterization = "theta")
anova(fit.lisrel, fit.mplus)

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.subject_clean: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Is there a way to get fitted scores for the residual/error term for each observation in a dataset, like how lavPredict gets scores for the latent variables? So, for example

model <- " latent =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 +x5 "

m1 <- cfa(model, data = df)

With this model, running predict(m1) would get me a predicted value of 'latent' for every observation in df. If, say, the residual variance in x5 not captured by 'latent' is of theoretical interest, can I capture that in the same way, so that every observation gets a non-'latent ' x5 score?

Really grateful for any advice, including on whether the premise of the question even makes sense!

messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrance and all,

Thank you for your reply.
I am still unsure how to specify the model. I will try to illustrate with a simplified example:
Say that I want to study factors that affect students' grades in 3 subjects (Y1, Y2 and Y3). The explanatory variables I will be testing have been measured in two levels: schools, and classes within those schools. For the schools I measured 3 variables (X1, X2 and X3), and for the classes I measured another three variables (M1, M2 and M3).

The following illustration shows the hypothesized paths from the conceptual model:

Which of the two following syntax is appropriate? :

Option 1:

m1 <- '
Level: 1
Y1 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
M3 ~ M1 + M2

Level: 2
Y1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
Y2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
Y3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
M1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
M2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
M3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
'

Option 2:

m2 <- '
Level: 1
Y1 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ M1 + M2 + M3
M3 ~ M1 + M2

Level: 2
Y1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3 +  M1 + M2 + M3
Y2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3  +  M1 + M2 + M3
Y3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3   +  M1 + M2 + M3
M1 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
M2 ~ X1 + X2 + X3
M3 ~ X1 + X2 + X3  + M2 + M3
'

Thanks in advance,
Efrat

On Sat, Oct 5, 2019 at 3:21 PM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > What I am unsure about is whether I need to specify the level-1 DVs in the level-2 equation?
>
> Every level-1 variable has a level-2 component (i.e., the cluster means) whose variance can only be modeled at level 2.  If you have no hypotheses about it, you could just allow it to covary with everything else at level 2, but it should be accounted for in your syntax
>
> > should I parameterize them with the same path coefficients as they have in the level-1 equation, or with new ones?
>
> Are you asking whether they need to be equal across levels?  No, process across levels can look very different.  Level-1 and -2 models do not have to have the same form, nor equal estimates of any parameters that are in both models.  But the data must be modeled (i.e., level-1 variables have level-2 components, period).
>

> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.body_plain:
Thanks again for the suggestions, Terrence. Unfortunately, neither of them solved the issue: thresholds were estimated in each model, and changing the ordered argument had no effect.

I tried to reproduce the example you gave, but with a bifactor structure in mod.cat (as is necessary in my applied case). Unfortunately, the model did not converge when using the datCat dataset, so I found a reproducible dataset with a bifactor structure here <http://rstudio-pubs-static.s3.amazonaws.com/9923_8c2532ee1f154554a7aa91e1ef8fe0fa.html>. After importing it, I added a column for gender, and renamed it datCat. When I then ran a version of your code, I still got the requires numeric/complex matrix/vector arguments error.

Is it possible that the error is generated when any bifactor model is tested? Perhaps, if you can reproduce what I did, you might be able to determine the cause; I have included my code here:

gist <- "https://gist.github.com/ericpgreen/7091485/raw/f4daec526bd69557874035b3c175b39cf6395408/simord.R"
source_url(gist, sha1="da165a61f147592e6a25cf2f0dcaa85027605290")
mydata[ , "g"] <- rep(c("M","F"),each=250)
mydata$g<-as.factor(mydata$g)
datCat<-mydata

mod.cat <http://mod.cat> <- '
   f1 =~ v1 + v2 + v3
   f2 =~ v4 + v5 + v6
   f3 =~ v7 + v8 + v9
   g1 =~ v9 + v8 + v7 + v6 + v5 + v4 + v3 + v2 + v1
   '

## configural model: no constraints across groups or repeated measures

syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat <http://mod.cat>, data = datCat,

                                ordered = paste0("v", 1:9),
                                parameterization = "theta", estimator = "WLSMV",

                                ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                                group = "g")
mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = datCat, group = "g",

                   ordered = paste0("v", 1:9), parameterization = "theta")
## equal thresholds

fit.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mod.cat <http://mod.cat>, data = datCat,

                             ordered = paste0("v", 1:9),
                             parameterization = "theta", estimator = "WLSMV",

                             ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                             group = "g", group.equal = "thresholds",
                             return.fit = TRUE)
myAFIs <- c("chisq","chisq.scaled","df","cfi.scaled","tli.scaled","rmsea.scaled","srmr")
out.thresh <- permuteMeasEq(nPermute = 10, uncon = fit.config, con = fit.thresh,
                             param = "thresholds", AFIs = myAFIs, moreAFIs = NULL)

messages.body_plain:
Call for Applications for:Assistant Professor of Research Methods
College of Education, Criminal Justice, and Human Services
University of Cincinnati

The School of Education in the College of Education, Criminal Justice, and Human Services is seeking applications for a tenure-track assistant professor position specializing in research, teaching and mentoring related to advanced research methodologies (e.g., quantitative/measurement, qualitative, statistics) in the context of education and social science research.  The prospective faculty member will have a primary appointment within the Research Methods area in the School of Education and is expected to maintain an active research agenda, teach introductory and advanced graduate courses in research methods and/or statistics, mentor graduate students, and contribute to service activities. messages.subject: Re: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.subject_clean: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way to get fitted scores for the residual/error term for each observation in a dataset, like how lavPredict gets scores for the latent variables?

No, but Jarrett Byrnes suggested some code that you could copy or download here to use:

https://github.com/simsem/semTools/pull/25/commits/07a2313937927e49185474f2113d9698eb315fb7

> can I capture that in the same way, so that every observation gets a non-'latent ' x5 score?

The problem with partialing the common factor from x5 is factor indeterminacy.  The factor scores are just estimates, based on estimated model parameters.  Different methods for estimating factor scores get you different estimates.  Accounting for the uncertainty of the factor-score estimates (and residuals implied by them) can be overcome by using a distribution of plausible values for factor scores instead of a single point estimate (see ?semTools::plausibleValues() and references therein) or by extending your model to avoid the issue (see below).

Not sure why you would need to partial out the common factor when you could just use the measurement model to have other variables (be) explain(ed by) x5's residual.  Search around for the MIMIC approach to testing DIF, and you might find that this is close to the kind of model you are looking for.  Here are examples from my grad student's work:

https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-77249-3_20

https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-018-1151-3

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: lavaan warns that a solution has NOT been found
messages.body_plain:
Can you also post the full error message, and any other warnings it produced?

Your sample size is quite small relative to the amount of data.  N = 159 yields only about 2 observations for each of 12*13/2 = 78 unique elements in the covariance matrix.  So it might be an empirical underidentification issue.

But the fact that the model converges on any of 10 (why not 12? Could you not remove 2 of them?) combinations of 11 items makes this seem more like a possible redundancy issue.  Try det(ang) to see if the determinant is positive.  If it is zero or negative, then the matrix is nonpositive definite, indicating probable linear dependencies among the variables.  Even though the largest correlation is only 0.64, there might be multicollinearity hiding somewhere (e.g., if you have all scale items AND the scale total in a correlation matrix).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject: Re: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.subject_clean: Get individual fitted residual scores
messages.body_plain:
> case_resid <- residuals(fit, type="casewise")

Indeed. How this works is as follows: first we compute factor scores for
all latent variables using lavPredict(). Then, we use the
factor-loadings to compute 'estimated' values for the observed
variables. The casewise residuals are the differences between the
observed and the estimated values for the observed variables.

However, there is a big caveat: the structural part (= any regressions
among latent variables) is completely ignored. See ?lavPredict and
https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/44 for more information about
this.

Nevertheless, it may be useful to detect outlying cases.

Yves.

I am conducting invariance testing for CFA I am doing. I have eight factors. So I can easily change the grouping variable and the factor I'm testing, I created variables in the code that I define prior to running it. Is there a way to turn the entirety of the code that uses these variables into a function so I don't have to have the analysis code written out 8 times?

Here is the first part of my code:

I made the group variable g1 which is "Q19" (gender), and the factor I'm testing is "cph" using data set "cfs"

g1 <- "Q19"
mft_fact <- cph

messages.subject: Re: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.subject_clean: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.body_plain:
The most common next step would be to test for partial invariance. This means to equate most  of the items in the factor, but not all of them, allowing the misbehaving items to be different between groups. Modification indices and lavtestscore are good ways to identify which items cannot be equated.

In the Bayesian SEM framework you could use approximate invariance, where the misbehaving items would be allowed to be closer, but not exactly the same, by adjusting the variance in the difference between parameters. You can use blavaan for this that uses similar syntax as lavaan

messages.subject: Re: R coding, creating an invariance testing function
messages.subject_clean: R coding, creating an invariance testing function
messages.body_plain:
> Is there a way to turn the entirety of the code that uses these variables into a function so I don't have to have the analysis code written out 8 times?

Sure, you can use mapply(measEq.syntax, parameterization="theta", SIMPLIFY = FALSE, ...)

And feed the varying arguments as vectors of character strings naming the objects you want.  You will just need to convert the strings to names and evaluate them.  Observe carefully how this works:

foo <- 7
bar <- "foo"
bar
as.name(bar)
eval(as.name(bar))

So you can use expand.grid() to cross the "factors", converting strings to names (except for g1, which needs to stay a string).  Here's a proof of concept you can use to adapt for your case:

## create some objects corresponding to your objects
for (i in 1:3) {
  assign(LETTERS[i], i) # the names of models for different factors
  assign(letters[i], -i) # the names of data.frames containing indicators
}
ls() # see there are objects named a, b, c, A, B, and C. Print them to see they are -1:-3 and 1:3.

## create all combinations
foo <- expand.grid(mft_fact = LETTERS[1:3],  # store your model-object names
                   mft_dat = letters[1:3],   # store your data.frame names
                   g1 = letters[4:5],        # store your grouping-variable names
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE) # make sure they remain characters
## for each column, create a list containing the evaluated names (i.e., models and data.frames)
mft_fact <- sapply(foo$mft_fact, function(x) eval(as.name(x)), simplify = FALSE)
mft_dat <- sapply(foo$mft_dat, function(x) eval(as.name(x)), simplify = FALSE)

When you replace "letters" and such with your actual information, you can print the last 2 lists to see your models and data.frames saved as list elements.  This way might make them look prettier:

lapply(mft_fact, cat)
lapply(mft_dat, head)

Finally, you can use mapply() to apply the function iteratively over the lists.  Anything that has only 1 constant value (like "theta") will be recycled.

mapply(measEq.syntax, parameterization="theta", SIMPLIFY = FALSE,
       configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat, group = foo$g1)

Of course, you can go even further by defining a custom function that fits several models and compares them using compareFit(), then mapply() that function to do everything at once.  Hopefully nothing breaks (e.g., if a single model doesn't converge).

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Thursday, October 10, 2019 at 5:33:23 AM UTC-5, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > Is there a way to turn the entirety of the code that uses these variables into a function so I don't have to have the analysis code written out 8 times?
>
> Sure, you can use mapply(measEq.syntax, parameterization="theta", SIMPLIFY = FALSE, ...)
>
> And feed the varying arguments as vectors of character strings naming the objects you want.  You will just need to convert the strings to names and evaluate them.  Observe carefully how this works:
>
> foo <- 7
> bar <- "foo"
> bar
> as.name(bar)
> eval(as.name(bar))
>
>
> So you can use expand.grid() to cross the "factors", converting strings to names (except for g1, which needs to stay a string).  Here's a proof of concept you can use to adapt for your case:
>
> ## create some objects corresponding to your objects
> for (i in 1:3) {
>   assign(LETTERS[i], i) # the names of models for different factors
>   assign(letters[i], -i) # the names of data.frames containing indicators
> }
> ls() # see there are objects named a, b, c, A, B, and C. Print them to see they are -1:-3 and 1:3.
>
>
> ## create all combinations
> foo <- expand.grid(mft_fact = LETTERS[1:3],  # store your model-object names
>                    mft_dat = letters[1:3],   # store your data.frame names
>                    g1 = letters[4:5],        # store your grouping-variable names
>                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE) # make sure they remain characters
> ## for each column, create a list containing the evaluated names (i.e., models and data.frames)
> mft_fact <- sapply(foo$mft_fact, function(x) eval(as.name(x)), simplify = FALSE)
> mft_dat <- sapply(foo$mft_dat, function(x) eval(as.name(x)), simplify = FALSE)
>
>
> When you replace "letters" and such with your actual information, you can print the last 2 lists to see your models and data.frames saved as list elements.  This way might make them look prettier:
>
> lapply(mft_fact, cat)
> lapply(mft_dat, head)
>
> Finally, you can use mapply() to apply the function iteratively over the lists.  Anything that has only 1 constant value (like "theta") will be recycled.
>
> mapply(measEq.syntax, parameterization="theta", SIMPLIFY = FALSE,
>        configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat, group = foo$g1)
>
> Of course, you can go even further by defining a custom function that fits several models and compares them using compareFit(), then mapply() that function to do everything at once.  Hopefully nothing breaks (e.g., if a single model doesn't converge).
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Need help from lavan pakage users (Reverese effect)
messages.body_plain:
You cannot estimate that model. The model is statistically not identified. In order to estimate the reciprocal effects of a on b and b on a, at the least either a or b will need a predictor which is unshared with the other variable (see Rigdon 1995). However, convention would allow for residual covariance between a and b. With free residual covariance, then both a and b will need a predictor not share with the other variable. I am not sure why lavaan has not detected the identification problem.

Rigdon, E. E. (1995). A necessary and sufficient identification rule for structural models estimated in practice. Multivariate behavioral research, 30(3), 359-383.

messages.subject_clean: bifactor CFA warning messages negative variances
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I would like to test a bifactor CFA model using lavaan, but I cannot eliminate negative variances and could not find the way to clear code to have a better model without warning messages.
(I did not have any issue in MPlus, where I received the following results: CFI = .980, TLI = .960, RMSEA = .080, df = 18, chi-square test: 46.016. I used MLR estimation there too.)
I used the following code in R:

# STUDY 1 - bifactor CFA
# model
model_G <- '
fac1      =~  NA*item1 + item2 + item5
fac2      =~  NA*item3 + item4 + item7
fac3      =~  NA*item6 + item8 + item9
G         =~  NA*item1 + item2 + item5 + item3 + item4 + item7 + item6 + item8 + item9
G         ~~ 0*fac1
G         ~~ 0*fac2
G         ~~ 0*fac3
fac1      ~~ 0*fac2
fac1      ~~ 0*fac3
fac2      ~~ 0*fac3
G         ~~ 1*G
fac1      ~~ 1*fac1
fac2      ~~ 1*fac2
fac3      ~~ 1*fac3
'

# fit, summary, values
fit_G <- cfa(model_G, data = study1, estimator = 'MLR', optim.force.converged = TRUE)
summary(fit_G, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

As you can see, I used "optim.force.converged = TRUE" because without it I received the following warning message:
Warning message:
In .local(object, ...) :
  lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge

Adding "optim.force.converged = TRUE" helped me to run the code, while I received even more warning messages:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_estimate(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavpartable = lavpartable,  :
  lavaan WARNING: the optimizer warns that a solution has NOT been found!
2: In lav_model_hessian(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING: Hessian is not fully symmetric. Max diff = 6.38485562376445e-06
3: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :
  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue
    (= -7.108829e-05) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that
    the model is not identified.
4: In lav_object_post_check(object) :
  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative
>

Do you have any suggestions how to modify my code to solve this issue in R?
I attached the relevant part of the data file and my code too. I hope it helps to reproduce the issue.

Thanks a lot for your suggestions in advance.
Janos

> I used "optim.force.converged = TRUE" because without it I received the following warning message:

> In .local(object, ...) :
>   lavaan WARNING: fit measures not available if model did not converge

That is not a good reason to use that argument.  It does not make your model converge, it simply tells lavaan to lie to you.  Read the description on the ?lavOptions help page:

logical. If TRUE, pretend the model has converged, no matter what.

You should only use this option if you know how to obtain useful information from the nonconverged model to help you resolve the convergence problem.

> Do you have any suggestions how to modify my code to solve this issue in R?

You can try leaving out the general factor to see if the model converges, or leaving out the method factors to see if that model converges.  You could also fix all general-factor loadings to 1, rather than estimate them.  Regardless, since some of your syntax is redundant with the std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE option, but I don't think that would be causing problems.

Hello,

I am trying to run a cross-lagged panel model with three time points and three variables of interest. Two of my variables (FREQ_DEP & CHRONO) are ordinal (4 levels) and one is continuous (OUTDOOR_SUMMER). I have an n of 5,000.

I am attempting to use this tutorial to fit the model with the pairwise maximum liklihood method: https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/pml/PL_Tutorial.pdf

Here is my code:

> > cl_chrono <-
> > '
> > #Regressions
> > FREQ_DEP_1~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0 + CHRONO_0
> > FREQ_DEP_2 ~  FREQ_DEP_1+ OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 + CHRONO_1
> > CHRONO_1 ~ CHRONO_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0 + FREQ_DEP_0
> > CHRONO_2 ~  CHRONO_1 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 + FREQ_DEP_1
> > OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 ~ FREQ_DEP_0 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_0 + CHRONO_0
> > OUTDOOR_SUMMER_2 ~  FREQ_DEP_1 + OUTDOOR_SUMMER_1 + CHRONO_1
> > '
> > fit_cl_chrono <- sem(cl_chrono, data=d, ordered=c("FREQ_DEP_1", "FREQ_DEP_2", "CHRONO_1", "CHRONO_2"), estimator='PML', std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = TRUE)

As you can see above, I declare the relevant endogenous variables as ordered.

When I run this model, I get the following error and am not sure what it means:

> > Error in pml_deriv1(Sigma.hat = Sigma.hat[[g]], Mu.hat = Mu.hat[[g]],  :
> >   lavaan ERROR: mixed + exo in PML not implemented; try optim.gradient = "numerical"

I have tried following its advice by adding "optim.gradient='numerical'" to my code but so far this model has taken ~20minutes to fit without completing.

I don't see how my data are any different to the tutorial so am unsure how to proceed and any guidance would be very much appreciated!

Thank you in advance and kind regards,

Angus

messages.body_plain:
> Now I know that parameterization is dramatically different for ordinal variables, but I have understood that, in terms of the overall DF, the differences "all come out in the wash," for a single-group model without specific constraints on the extra parameters.

Not really, just by coincidence in many circumstances, such as when all your factors are at least just-identified.

>      I (eventually) use parametertable() to track down the "extra" free parameter. That output appears to show the two structural paths constrained to equality being counted as 2 separate free parameters, if I am reading the "free" column correctly. But this is so for both outputs, so maybe that is not the real source of the discrepancy(?).

It is not.  The different numbers for equality-constrained parameters get compensated for by counting the constraints at the bottom of the parameter table (where $op == "==").

The source of the discrepancy is that in ML, your residual variances are free parameters, only one of which must be fixed (for single indicator y1), whereas they are all already fixed == 1 in DWLS.  The thresholds "wash out" (saturated, like mean structure is in the ML case), and here is the count for DWLS fitted to polychoric correlations:

unique observed polychoric correlations                  7*(7-1) / 2 = 21
- 1 free loading per observed (when std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)                   -  7

- 1 for the two structural paths constrained to equality             -  1
- 1 for the free covariance between f1 and f2                        -  1

                                                                       12  DF

Terrence, thanks a lot for your quick reply and suggestions.
I felt (and now see it why) that using forced converge is not a good practice, I deleted it from the code.

I also cleared the redundancies: I defined std.lv <http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fstd.lv&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHvA0OtSuL0EhXvTEm3tuvtsMDsmg>=TRUE instead of fixing covariances to zero on by one. Lavaan tutorial states that "If the argument std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE is used, the factor loadings of the first indicator of each latent variable will no longer be fixed to 1."
If I understand it right, defining each factor loading as unknown (pre-multiplying with NA) is also a redundancy, so I deleted them too.
After these modifications, using this code:

# STUDY 1 - bifactor CFA
# model
model_G <- '

fac1      =~  item1 + item2 + item5
fac2      =~  item3 + item4 + item7
fac3      =~  item6 + item8 + item9
G         =~  item1 + item2 + item5 + item3 + item4 + item7 + item6 + item8 + item9

G         ~~ 1*G
fac1      ~~ 1*fac1
fac2      ~~ 1*fac2
fac3      ~~ 1*fac3
'
# fit, summary, values

fit_G <- cfa(model_G, data = study1, estimator = 'MLR', std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)

summary(fit_G, fit.measures = TRUE, standardized = TRUE)

I still receive the following warning messages:
Warning messages:
1: In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel2, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats,  :

  lavaan WARNING:
    The variance-covariance matrix of the estimated parameters (vcov)
    does not appear to be positive definite! The smallest eigenvalue

    (= -2.757799e-04) is smaller than zero. This may be a symptom that

    the model is not identified.

2: In lav_object_post_check(object) :

  lavaan WARNING: some estimated ov variances are negative

Leaving out either the general factor or the method factors works, the models converge without warning messages. Fixing all general-factor loadings to 1 leads a not converged model again.

The fit indices of the above showed bifactor model are much better (CFI = .990, TLI = .970, RMSEA = .069, df = 12, chi-square test: 25.870) than the first-order, second-order, or the general factor only models.
And the following MPlus code works without any problem, and gives the following results: CFI = .980, TLI = .960, RMSEA = .080, df = 18, chi-square test: 46.016

 ANALYSIS:
      estimator = mlr;
  !only for sample 1
      iteration = 10000;
      h1iteration = 10000;
      convergence = .05;
      h1convergence = .05;

 MODEL:
      global BY item2* item1 item3 item4 item5 item6 item7 item8 item9;

      fac1 BY item1* item2 item5;
      fac2 BY item3* item4 item7;
      fac3 BY item6* item8 item9;

      global@1; fac1@1; fac2@1; fac3@1;

      global-fac3 WITH global-fac3@0;

Unfortunately, I still do not know what makes the difference between the MPlus and R results, maybe fixing the problems suggested in the warning messages would solve the issue.

messages.body_plain:
You must make sure that the 'specific' factors are uncorrelated with the
'global' factor. In Mplus, you had the syntax line

global-fac3 WITH global-fac3@0;

which sets ALL covariances to zero. In lavaan, you can either write

global ~~ 0*fac1 + 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac1 ~~ 0*fac2 + 0*fac3
fac2 ~~ 0*fac3

or use the orthgonal = TRUE argument.

Yves.

messages.subject: Re: Simulate multilevel SEM with simsem?
messages.subject_clean: Simulate multilevel SEM with simsem?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Terrence,

thank you very much for your explanation and insights, and sorry for my delayed response.
I have tried to create a function to simulate multilevel multivariate data based on your suggestions, which returns the parameters estimated by a MCFA model specified on the simulated data.

If matrices.type="simulated", the function uses the loadings specified in the "level1.model" and "level2.model" arguments to simulate data (using simulateData) on both levels, separately. Then, the covariance matrices on both levels are saved and used to simulate the BLUPs and the residuals.
If matrices.type="empirical", the covariance matrices are computed from an existing dataset over which the MCFA model is specified.
Then, the two multivariate datasets are "added" (as you said) to create the multilevel dataset from which the parameters are estimated and saved.

It took a long time (I'm not used to write functions), but it seems to work under different conditions (e.g., with more than one latent variable, free loadings on both levels), and I would really appreciate receiving your feedback on it. Also, I hope the function can be useful for other lavaan users aiming to simulate multilevel SEM data.

Best Regards,
Luca

MCFAsim <- function(N_2=100,   # number of clusters (level 2)
                    N_1=10,    # number of observations(level 1)
                    MU=0,      # grand average
                    n.items=4, # number of items to be generated
                    item.letter="x", # letter that identifies items of interest
                    cluster="ID",   # name of the grouping variable

                    # COVARIANCE MATRICES
                    matrices.type="simulated", # simulated or empirical
                    std=TRUE, # standardized cov matrices?
                    # 2.1. if empirical, specify the DATASET and the cluster variable
                    mydata=NA, # dataset (data.frame)
                    # 2.2. if simulated, specify the LOADINGS in the one-level model(s)
                    level2.model="WLb =~ 0.6*x1 + 0.6*x2 + 0.6*x3 + 0.6*x4",
                    level1.model=level2.model, # default: the same as level 1 (conf. construct)

                    # MCFA MODEL
                    twolevels.model='level: 1
                                     WLw =~ a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3 + d*x4
                                     level: 2
                                     WLb =~ a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3 + d*x4',

                    corrs=FALSE # want to save also correlations between simulated variables?
){

  if(matrices.type=="simulated"){
    # generate data on lv2
    myData <- lavaan::simulateData(level2.model,model.type="cfa",std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,sample.nobs=N_2)
    b.cov <- lavaan::inspectSampleCov(level2.model,myData)$'cov' # cov matrix on lv2
    # generate data on lv1
    myData <- lavaan::simulateData(level1.model,model.type="cfa",std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE,sample.nobs=N_1)
    w.cov <- lavaan::inspectSampleCov(level2.model,myData)$'cov' # covariance matrix on lv1

    }else if(matrices.type=="empirical"){
      # take cov matrices from observed data using the specified MCFA model
      b.cov <- lavaan::inspectSampleCov(twolevels.model,mydata,cluster="ID")$ID$`cov`
      w.cov <- lavaan::inspectSampleCov(twolevels.model,mydata,cluster="ID")$`within`$`cov`
    }

  # standardized cov matrices?
  if(std==TRUE){
    b.cov <- cov2cor(b.cov)
    w.cov <- cov2cor(w.cov)
  }

  # Simulating clusters' means (lv2) = grandAverage + BLUP
  U <- MASS::mvrnorm(n=N_2,mu=rep(0,n.items),Sigma=b.cov) # BLUPs
  cMeans <- MU + U # simulated clusters' means (1 X cluster X item)

  # Simulating within-cluster scores (lv1) = clusters' means + residual deviance
  dataList <- list()
  for (cl in 1:nrow(cMeans)){
    e <- MASS::mvrnorm(n=N_1,mu=rep(0,n.items),Sigma=w.cov) # Residuals
    for (i in 1:nrow(e)){ e[i,] <- e[i,] + cMeans[cl,] } # within-cluster scores
    dataList[[cl]] <- e
  }

  # Merging lv1 and lv2 data in a multilevel dataset
  simulated <- data.frame(ID=rep(1:N_2,N_1),TIME=rep(rep(NA,N_1),N_2)) # empty dataset
  simulated <- simulated[order(simulated$ID),] # ordered by ID
  simulated$TIME=rep(1:N_1,N_2)
  for(i in 1:n.items){ simulated <- cbind(simulated,rep(NA,nrow(simulated))) } # empty items columns
  colnames(simulated)[3:ncol(simulated)] <- paste(item.letter,seq(1,n.items,1),sep="") # item names
  for(cl in 1:length(dataList)){ # from list to df
    simulated[simulated$ID==cl,3:ncol(simulated)] <- dataList[[cl]]
  }

  # parameters estimation
  results <- try(lavaan::cfa(twolevels.model,data=simulated,cluster=cluster,std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE),silent=TRUE) # CFA
  parameters <- data.frame(matrix(nrow=0,ncol=n.items*6+5+3+6)) # empty dataset

  if(class(results)!="try-error"){ error = FALSE # errors check
    if(lavaan::lavInspect(results,"converged")==TRUE){ convergence = TRUE # convergence check
      if(any(as.vector(lavaan::lavInspect(results,"est")[["ID"]][["theta"]])<0) & # negative var check
         any(as.vector(lavaan::lavInspect(results,"est")[["within"]][["theta"]])<0)){
        neg.Variance = TRUE } else { neg.Variance = FALSE }

    parameters <- rbind(parameters,
                          # model info (ncol=5)
                        c(N_2,N_1,matrices.type,lavaan::lavInspect(results,"fit")[c("npar")],std,
                          # converg. (ncol=3)
                          error,convergence,neg.Variance,
                          # lv1 & lv2 loadings - default type="std.all" (ncol=n.items*2)
                          c(round(lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)[
                            lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)$op=="=~","est.std"],3)),
                          # fit indices (ncol=6)
                          round(lavaan::lavInspect(results,"fit")[c("chisq","df","rmsea","cfi",
                                                                    "srmr_within","srmr_between")],3),
                          # lv1&lv2 loadings CI (ncol=n.items*4)
                          c(round(lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)[
                            lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)$op=="=~","ci.lower"],3)),
                          c(round(lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)[
                            lavaan::standardizedsolution(results)$op=="=~","ci.upper"],3))

                          # correlations between observed variables
                          ))

    }else{ convergence = FALSE # not converged
    parameters <- rbind(parameters,
                        c(N_2,N_1,matrices.type,NA,std, # model info (ncol=5)
                          error,convergence,NA, # converg. (ncol=3)
                          rep(NA,n.items*6+6))) # loadings and fit indices (ncol=n.items*4+4)
    }
  }else{ error=TRUE # error
  parameters <- rbind(parameters,
                      c(N_2,N_1,matrices.type,NA,std, # model info (ncol=2)
                        error,NA,NA, # converg. (ncol=3)
                        rep(NA,n.items*6+6))) # loadings and fit indices (ncol=n.items*4+4)
    }

  colnames(parameters) <- c("N_2","N_1","matrices.type","npar","std","error","converged","negVariance",
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("w",n.items),sep=""),
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("b",n.items),sep=""),
                            "chisq","df","rmsea","cfi","srmr_between","srmr_within",
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("w.CI.low",n.items),sep=""),
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("b.CI.low",n.items),sep=""),
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("w.CI.up",n.items),sep=""),
                            paste(paste(item.letter,1:n.items,sep=""),rep("b.CI.up",n.items),sep=""))

  if(corrs==TRUE){ # should add n.items*(n-1)/2 columns
    corrS <- cor(simulated[,3:ncol(simulated)],simulated[,3:ncol(simulated)],use="complete.obs",method="pearson")
    corr.lab <- matrix(apply(expand.grid(rownames(corrS),rownames(corrS)),1,paste,collapse="."),
                       nrow=n.items,ncol=n.items)
    corrS <- round(corrS[lower.tri(corrS, diag = FALSE)],2)
    names(corrS) <- corr.lab[lower.tri(corr.lab, diag = FALSE)]
    parameters <- cbind(parameters,t(corrS))
  }

  return(parameters)

  }

Il giorno giovedì 27 giugno 2019 22:30:04 UTC+2, Terrence Jorgensen ha scritto:
> > I did not get what you mean with "add" in step 3
>
> For simplicity, look at a univariate intercept-only multilevel model:
>
> y_{ij} = mu + u_j + e_{ij}
>
> The observed variable y for person i in cluster j is a sum of 3 components:
> mu is a grand mean of cluster means
> u_j is the deviation of cluster j's mean from mu
> within cluster j, e_{ij} is the deviation of individual i's score from cluster j's mean
> u_j and e_{ij} are both normally distributed with means = 0 and variances = tau^2 for clusters and sigma^2 for individuals.  In practice, you can simulate data for N_2 clusters by generating N_2 cluster means from a normal distribution with M = mu and SD = tau
>
> set.seed(123)
> cMeans <- rnorm(N_2, m = mu, SD = tau)
>
>
> That's the same as generating a vector of U from a distribution with mean = 0, then adding mu + U.
>
> set.seed(123)
> U <- rnorm(N_2, m = 0, SD = tau)
> cMeans <- mu + U
>
> Then you could loop over clusters to generate Level-1 residuals for N_1 individuals within each cluster (assuming a constant cluster size; otherwise, loop over a vector of N_2 cluster sizes) and add it to the cluster mean.
>
> dataList <- list()
> for (cl in 1:N_2) {
>   e <- rnorm(N_1, m = 0, sd = sigma)
>   dataList[[cl]] <- cMeans[cl] + e
>   ## same as mu + U[cl] + e
>   ## recognize the equation?
> }
>
> That is what I meant, but on a multivariate level.  You can replace mu with a mean vector, tau and sigma by covariance matrices at L1 and L2, and rnorm() by MASS::mvrnorm()
>
> > I was wandering if a reasonable solution would be to focus my power analysis exclusively on the between-individuals level
>
> Only if that is the model you will run to test your hypothesis.  The whole point of a simulation is to simulate what you are going to do, but under known conditions.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

fit <- sem(model = model, data = PRETEND_DATA)

It sounds like just want to get a path diagram based on your correspondence with Yves.

If so,
semPaths(fit)

might be what you want instead of the data argument.

messages.body_plain:
Terrence--
     Thank you. I'll exploit a coincidence, as a simplification, if it is reliable. It looks like my prior examples had all involved factors with multiple indicators. Narrow thinking will get you every time.
--Ed Rigdon

On Tue, Oct 22, 2019 at 1:59 AM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Now I know that parameterization is dramatically different for ordinal variables, but I have understood that, in terms of the overall DF, the differences "all come out in the wash," for a single-group model without specific constraints on the extra parameters.
>
> Not really, just by coincidence in many circumstances, such as when all your factors are at least just-identified.
>
> >      I (eventually) use parametertable() to track down the "extra" free parameter. That output appears to show the two structural paths constrained to equality being counted as 2 separate free parameters, if I am reading the "free" column correctly. But this is so for both outputs, so maybe that is not the real source of the discrepancy(?).
>
> It is not.  The different numbers for equality-constrained parameters get compensated for by counting the constraints at the bottom of the parameter table (where $op == "==").
>
> The source of the discrepancy is that in ML, your residual variances are free parameters, only one of which must be fixed (for single indicator y1), whereas they are all already fixed == 1 in DWLS.  The thresholds "wash out" (saturated, like mean structure is in the ML case), and here is the count for DWLS fitted to polychoric correlations:
>
> unique observed polychoric correlations                  7*(7-1) / 2 = 21
> - 1 free loading per observed (when std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)                   -  7
> - 1 for the two structural paths constrained to equality             -  1
> - 1 for the free covariance between f1 and f2                        -  1
>                                                                        12  DF
>
>

messages.body_plain:
> I also cleared the redundancies: I defined std.lv <http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fstd.lv&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNHvA0OtSuL0EhXvTEm3tuvtsMDsmg>=TRUE instead of fixing covariances to zero on by one.

You were confusing std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE with orthogonal=TRUE

> defining each factor loading as unknown (pre-multiplying with NA) is also a redundancy, so I deleted them too.

(when std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE) Correct.

> Leaving out either the general factor or the method factors works, the models converge without warning messages.

Perhaps the bifactor model is not appropriate.  Even if it is, they are notorious for empirical underidentification problems (factor loading matrix is not full rank), leading to convergence issues or Heywood cases (you are experiencing both).

> I still do not know what makes the difference between the MPlus and R results, maybe fixing the problems suggested in the warning messages would solve the issue.

Yves has done quite a job making sure lavaan can reproduce Mplus results to the third decimal for continuous indicators.  Would you be able to share data and both the Mplus and lavaan scripts fitting the same bifactor model that you say does not yield problems in Mplus?  Or at least your Mplus output file and lavaan's summary() output, so we can see how the solutions compare?

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

I see that a now has x3 as a predictor while b now has x4 as a predictor. The coefficients for x3 and x4 in these equations must be large. I suggest estimating a model without the reciprocal effects, to make sure that the coefficients are substantial in that case. You might use those estimates as starting values in the reciprocal relations model. Sometimes the iterative estimation process gets stuck in a bad patch of parameter space. If you can provide good starting values (not near 0, and on the correct side of 0), that will sometimes help you to achieve convergence

messages.body_plain:
Have a look at the mediation page on the Mplus website: https://www.statmodel.com/Mediation.shtml.  There you’ll find links to Preacher’s Mplus code for models described in Preacher et al. (2010), including 1-1-1. Also have a look at the “Figure it Out” site by Chris Stride linked to that page—it’s a fantastic resource for migrating from Process.  Adapting Mplus code to lavaan is pretty straightforward. I haven’t tried it but the mplus2lavaan function (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/mplus2lavaan.html) might also be helpful.

I should also mention Moon’s ProcessR package and shiny page at https://rpubs.com/cardiomoon/468602.  It’s meant to be the R version of Process and estimates most Process models with lavaan.  You can adapt the code as needed.

Here's an example to get you started:

I adapted Preacher’s MSEM 1-1-1 Mplus code to lavaan.  See: https://www.statmodel.com/download/Preacher.pdf.

I used Mplus data example 9.5 and renamed the variables so that they correspond to Preacher. The data weren’t meant to illustrate multilevel mediation but it works well enough to see how to model it.

mp <- read.table("https://www.statmodel.com/usersguide/chap9/ex9.5.dat")

head(mp)

names(mp) <- c("y","y2","x","m","w","clus")

library(lavaan)

model <- '

level: 1
y ~ x + bw*m
m ~ aw*x

level: 2
y ~ x + bb*m
m ~ ab*x

indw := aw*bw
indb := ab*bb
'

model.out <- sem(model, data = mp, cluster = "clus")

summary(model.out)

messages.body_plain:
Hi János,

As Terrence indicated, bifactor models have an unfortunate tendency to display convergence issues (and sometimes converged models have obviously incorrect estimates). Depending on the reason you are fitting the bifactor model, there are a number of ways to overcome this problem:

(1) You can leave off a specific factor or even just a single item (and, if you like, allow the other specific factors to correlate). This is the approach of Eid et al. (2017). This approach is reasonable when one of the specific factors can reasonably be expected to be trivial because its content is so closely aligned with the general factor.

(2) If your purpose is checking if your data is unidimensional to be treated as such (per Rodriguez, Reise, & Haviland, 2016), then if you accept the three factor model as fitting acceptably, you can reparameterize it into a special case of bifactor model called a "testlet" model. You can either directly compute the coefficients from the three factor model, or you can fit a model in which factor loadings are constrained to be equal in the general and specific factors, the general factor variance is fixed to one, and the specific factor variances are freely estimated.

Note that this approach is only reasonable for two or three factor models (testlet models are statistically equivalent to second order factor models, and two- and three- factor correlated traits models are always statistically equivalent to second order factor models).

(3) If you plan on using a total sum score eventually, then you can follow Terrence's suggestion above and fix all the loadings of the general factor to one.

(4) If you are willing to switch to a Bayesian framework you have some more choices

(5) You can resolve the convergence issue in a number of other creative ways, but you'd be hard pressed to argue that other techniques are reasonable.

It has been my personal, anecdotal experience (i.e., take this with a grain of salt) that misfit is often to blame for bifactor models having convergence issues. To diagnose if this is actually the case, I would fit a unidimensional model and look at the residual correlation matrix. The within specific factor residual correlation should be large and the across specific factor residual correlations should be small.

-David

Eid, M., Geiser, C., Koch, T., & Heene, M. (2017). Anomalous results in G-factor models: Explanations and alternatives. Psychological Methods, 22(3), 541.
Rodriguez, A., Reise, S. P., & Haviland, M. G. (2016). Evaluating bifactor models: calculating and interpreting statistical indices. Psychological Methods, 21(2), 137.

Hi,

Have a look at the mediation page on the Mplus website: https://www.statmodel.com/Mediation.shtml.  There you’ll find links to Preacher’s Mplus code for models described in Preacher et al. (2010), including 1-1-1. Also have a look at the “Figure it Out” site by Chris Stride linked to that page—it’s a fantastic resource for migrating from Process.  Adapting Mplus code to lavaan is pretty straightforward. I haven’t tried it but the mplus2lavaan function (https://rdrr.io/cran/lavaan/man/mplus2lavaan.html) might also be helpful.

I should also mention Moon’s ProcessR package and shiny page at https://rpubs.com/cardiomoon/468602.  It’s meant to be the R version of Process and estimates most Process models with lavaan.  You can adapt the code as needed.

Best,

Joe

messages.subject: Re: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.subject_clean: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.body_plain:
> Now that I have metric invariance or partial metric invariance for all my factors, I want to compare factor means. Is there any problem with me just entering the code from freeing these parameters into the model syntax I use for comparing factor means?

It is highly dubious to constrain an item's intercepts to equality if its loadings are not constrained.  That is analogous to estimating an interaction term (here, ce by Q19) without including a main effect (of Q19), if you had observed ce to include as a predictor in a regression model for item Q2_1.

Your syntax indicates you freed the loadings of Q2_1, so free their intercepts too.  Either in the syntax (Q2_1 ~ c(int2.g1, int2.g2)*1 ) or using group.partial = "Q2_1~1"

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Dear All,
I'm trying to use lavaan to do a cfa for ordered variables and I get good results but also a warning message: covariance matrix of lv not defined positive. I saw Jeremias answer to João Maroco and I have exactly the same problema.

In thart answer, Jeremias talk about Cholesky decomposition:

I'll write something about the Cholesky later, but here's an example to get you going:

## Regular example:
## The famous Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

Same data, but model covariances of speed, textual and visual using Cholesky.

HS.model2 <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9
              c1 =~ visual + textual + speed
              c2 =~ textual + speed
              c3 =~ speed
              c1 ~~ 0*c2 + 0*c3
              c2 ~~ 0*c3
              visual ~~ 0 * visual
              textual ~~ 0 * textual
              speed ~~ 0 * speed'

I have tried to use this but I got the same warning message, My questions are:

- Is this exemple using Cholesky correct?
- Using this model using Cholesky I can use the same sintaxe to apply CFA: fit<-cfa(model, data=…, ordered=C(…))

I appreciate any help to overcome this problem.

Best, Ana

Niels Waller
University of Minnesota

https://support.sas.com/documentation/cdl/en/statug/63033/HTML/default/viewer.htm#statug_tcalis_sect094.htm

mod04 = '
  # loadings of MVs on LVs in Lambda (L)
    G        =~ G01*X1 + G02*X2 + G03*X3 +
                    G04*X4 + G05*X5 + G06*X6 +
                    G07*X7 + G08*X8 + G09*X9

    F1  =~ L01*X1  + L02*X2  +  L03*X3
    F2  =~ L04*X4  + L05*X5  +  L06*X6
    F3  =~ L07*X7 +  L08*X8 +   L09*X9

  # unique factor variances for MVs
    X1  ~~ X1
    X2  ~~ X2
    X3  ~~ X3
    X4  ~~ X4
    X5  ~~ X5
    X6  ~~ X6
    X7  ~~ X7
    X8  ~~ X8
    X9  ~~ X9

  # LV variances and covariances in Psi (P)
    G  ~~ 1*G
    F1 ~~ 1*F1
    F2 ~~ 1*F2
    F3 ~~ 1*F3

    F1 ~~ 0*G
    F2 ~~ 0*G + 0*F1
    F3 ~~ 0*G + 0*F1 + 0*F2

  # constraints
  # This is what I would like to do
         G01 == a*L01
         G02 == a*L02
         G03 == a*L03

         G04 == b*L04
         G05 == b*L05
         G06 == b*L06

         G07 == c*L07
         G08 == c*L08
         G09 == c*L09

 '

Niels,
a, b and c appear to be constraining the ratios of G to L for pairs of items within specific factors.  Could you impose the constraints without these added parameters as shown below?  Caveat, you did not provide a runable example, so I have only tested with lavaanify() and not by estimating the model.

Keith

require(lavaan)

mod04_modified = '

  # loadings of MVs on LVs in Lambda (L)
    G        =~ G01*X1 + G02*X2 + G03*X3 +
                    G04*X4 + G05*X5 + G06*X6 +
                    G07*X7 + G08*X8 + G09*X9

    F1  =~ L01*X1  + L02*X2  +  L03*X3
    F2  =~ L04*X4  + L05*X5  +  L06*X6
    F3  =~ L07*X7 +  L08*X8 +   L09*X9

  # unique factor variances for MVs
    X1  ~~ X1
    X2  ~~ X2
    X3  ~~ X3
    X4  ~~ X4
    X5  ~~ X5
    X6  ~~ X6
    X7  ~~ X7
    X8  ~~ X8
    X9  ~~ X9

  # LV variances and covariances in Psi (P)
    G  ~~ 1*G
    F1 ~~ 1*F1
    F2 ~~ 1*F2
    F3 ~~ 1*F3

    F1 ~~ 0*G
    F2 ~~ 0*G + 0*F1
    F3 ~~ 0*G + 0*F1 + 0*F2

  # constraints
  # This is what I would like to do

  #       G01 == a*L01
  #       G02 == a*L02
  #       G03 == a*L03
    G01 == L01 * G02 / L02
    G02 == L02 * G03 / L03

  #       G04 == b*L04
  #       G05 == b*L05
  #       G06 == b*L06
    G04 == L04 * G05 / L05
    G05 == L05 * G06 / L06

  #       G07 == c*L07
  #       G08 == c*L08
  #       G09 == c*L09
    G07 == L07 * G08 / L08
    G08 == L08 * G09 / L09

 ' # end mod04_modified

 lavaanify(mod04_modified)

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ l1v * x1 + l2v * 1 * x2 + x3

              # Constructed parameters

              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=FALSE,

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am trying to run a multilevel moderated mediation in lavaan with all level 1 variables. I have a response variable (Resp), a mediator (Med), a predictor (Pred), and a moderator (Mod), all nested within subjects.

I have found relevant resources on lavaan that have provided syntax for mediation, moderated mediation, and multilevel SEM, but not all of these things combined for moderated multilevel mediation. Some of such links are below:
http://www.da.ugent.be/cvs/pages/en/Presentations/Presentation%20Yves%20Rosseel.pdf
https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/zurich2017/MULTILEVEL/lavaan_multilevel_zurich2017.pdf
http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/lavaan/6oUYvCTxJzY
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/163436/r-moderated-mediation-using-the-lavaan-package

I understand that the lavaan syntax for specifying multilevel SEM is '
level: 1
...
level: 2
...
'
summary(... cluster = "cluster")

While all of this makes sense, it seems to require that you have some variables included in level 2. However, my multilevel moderated mediation is all level 1 variables. So when I try to run:
lavMed <- '
level: 1
  # direct effect
  Resp ~ c*Pred
  # mediator
  Med ~ a*Pred
  Resp ~ b*Med
  # indirect effect (a*b)
  ab := a*b
  # total effect
  total := c + (a*b)
level: 2
'

I unfortunately get an error that I need syntax at level 2.

I am not sure if this is correct but then I try just an intercept at level 2 since I am not using any level 2 variables in the model... Just nesting level 1 variables in subjects to account for non-independence/clustering.

lavMed <- '
level: 1
  # direct effect
  Resp ~ c*Pred
  # mediator
  Med ~ a*Pred
  Resp ~ b*Med
  # indirect effect (a*b)
  ab := a*b
  # total effect
  total := c + (a*b)
level: 2
  subID ~ 1
'
fit <- sem(lavMed,
           data = medDf,
           group = "Mod", cluster = "subID")
summary(fit)

When I run this, I get:
Error in ov.names.l[[g]] : subscript out of bounds

I am pretty stumped now. Why am I getting this error? How can I run a multilevel moderated mediation in lavaan, that does not use any level 2 variables? Is the syntax on the right track? Any help would be greatly appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
It looks to me like you are wanting to fit a bifactor model with testlet constraints. I've not done that in lavaan before, but I imagine that the strategy I use to fit such models in Mplus will work fine:

(1) Give loadings for the same item the same label in both the general and specific factor
(2) Assign a variance of 1 to the general factor
(3) Allow the specific factor variances to be freely estimated

This is how testlet IRT models were parameterized to facilitate their estimation before the dimensionality reduction trick was discovered.

-David

messages.subject: RE: Cholesky decomposition
messages.subject_clean: Cholesky decomposition
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

It means that some of your latent variables have negative estimated variance or a null correlation with other latent variables. It can not be. By definition variances are positive… but the SEM uses maximization algorithms to minimize the discrepancy function, and that’s why you can get negative variances – that is the math solution that minimizes the discrepancy function. In the same line, the covariances between LV that minimize the discrepancy can be zero or close to zero… and that is a problem because the variance-covariance matrix needs to be inverted to generate parameters’ SE and tests…

How to solve it:

Use lavInspect(fit, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>") or  inspect(fit, what = "cor.lv <http://cor.lv>")
find the negative variances and 0 or close to 0 covariances
Look at the indicators of the latent variables for differences in scale formats (0-10 or 0-100 makes a difference… if that is the case reduce everything to the same scale format…
If you are using categorical indicators and WLSMV estimation, increase your sample size so that you have enough observations in each category of the categorical indicator…
Go for corrective measures.
If variances are negative, fix them to a small value something like lv~~0.1*lv or something like

lv ~~ a*lv

a > 0
If covariances are 0, reformulate your model. Are you sure that all the lv are required?
If you want to dig in the proportions of shared variance (covariance) by the different lv, than do a Cholesky decomposition as Jeremias proposed. Note that the Cholesky decomposition does not solve the problem, only gives clues to why covariances are null, and variances are negative…

Hope this helps!

Best,

João Marôco

messages.body_plain:
That depends on what you wish to depict. If B and C have no connection except through A, then use nothing between B and C. If there is residual covariance between B and C after accounting for the covariance due to their joining dependence on A, then convention represents that using a curved double-headed arrow. If you mean that B or C has an effect on the other, then use an arrow with one head.

messages.subject_clean: Conflicting Beta Signs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I just ran a simple (standard) mediation model, where A has a direct effect on B, with a mediator M.

[path c]: A predicts B - positive beta.
[path a]: A predicts M - positive beta.
[path b]: M predicts B - negative beta.

[indirect ab]: A-M-B - negative.

All are significant (p < 0.05).

What does this mean (i.e., conflicting beta signs), and how should I go about interpreting this mediation model?

Thank you in advance!

messages.subject: Re: Conflicting Beta Signs
messages.subject_clean: Conflicting Beta Signs
messages.body_plain:
I understand this kind of result as possible non-transitivity in results. Non-transitivity occurs when positively correlated variables have inverse relations to a 3rd variable. Of course you want to check the confidence intervals to be sure the values are truly different to zero. But when the correlation between the variables is not high it is possible to discover non-transitivity. This type of phenomenon is quite feasible as long as the correlations are sufficiently different from 1 (Langford, Schwertman, & Owens, 2001). However, structural equation approaches can
help deal with cases where the correlations among predictors are large (Maruyama, 1998).
Langford, E., Schwertman, N., & Owens, M. (2001). Is the property of being positively correlated transitive? The American Statistician, 55(4), 322–325. doi:10.1198/000313001753272286
Maruyama, G. M. (1998). Basics of Structural Equation Modeling. Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage.

What you are looking for is longitudinal measurement invariance. You do the configural, weak, and strong invariance tests across time instead of groups. Once strong invariance has been established you can test mean chnage over time by either comparing means or doing a growth curve model of the factor means

You can check the following books, I believe Little has lavaan code examples, while Grimm and McArdle have OpenMx code examples fro R

Grimm, K. J., Ram, N., & Estabrook, R. (2016). Growth Modeling: Structural Equation and Multilevel Modeling Approaches. New York, NY, US.
Little, T. D. (2013). Longitudinal Structural Equation Modeling. New York, NY, US: The Guilford Press.
McArdle, J. J., & Nesselroade, J. R. (2014). Longitudinal data analysis using structural equation models. https://doi.org/10.1037/14440-000

Further to Mauricio's answer
McCardle argues in repeated measures data it is sufficient to have configural and metric invariance between times. His view is that as events change things over time it is likely that the item intercepts should change as a consequence of those events. Hence, requiring strong invariance might not be necessary. see
McArdle, J. J. (2007). Five steps in the structural factor analysis of longitudinal data. In R. Cudeck & R. C. MacCallum (Eds.), Factor analysis at 100: Historical developments and future directions (pp. 99-130). Mahwah, NJ: LEA.
